lines.text: I wrote them down that night, by candlelight, in the back of my copy of the Charter of Aldric. It seemed the right book.

Col Wick, from Saltmouth, who was sixteen and had told the muster he was eighteen. Brenna Fell, who kept bees behind the mill. Old Teodor Marsh, who was far too old to be there, and knew it, and came anyway.
Halla and Eirik, two Skeld cousins, on the same rock, an hour apart. Twenty names. Every one of them a thread I had felt go out.
At dawn, Wren, Oswin, Tamsin and Ilse rode for Saltmouth and Pell's fastest ship. Midwinter was sixteen days away.
If you come down to the gate to say goodbye, I'll shoot you. Go and see the families. That's your job. This is ours.
So I went to see the families. All of them. Every house, every tent, every boat.
It took eleven days. Some lived in Saltmouth, some in Kesting. Two Skeld families lived so far out on the ice that Kell had to guide me.
He was sixteen. He told you he was eighteen, didn't he? He told everyone that.
He did. I believed him. I'm sorry.
She hit me. Not hard. Then she held on to me and cried, and I let her, because that was what I'd come for.
Brenna Fell's husband gave me a pot of honey and asked me to eat with them. I did. Nobody said much. The honey was very good.
The Skeld don't bury their dead. They give them to the White, on a sledge, with their spear and their best furs. Halla's grandmother let me pull the sledge.
You came yourself, Warm One. Southern lords send letters.
Old Teodor had no family left at all. So I sat in his empty house for an hour and told it thank you. It seemed better than nothing.
Is my papa coming back, Lord Lucan?
I had promised Bram once that I would bring them all back. I couldn't lie to her.
No. He isn't. But I'll come back. Every year, on this day. I promise you that.
On the eleventh night I came home and sat down to write the twentieth letter. I don't remember finishing it.
Bram found me at dawn, asleep at the desk with my cheek on the Charter. He put his own cloak over my shoulders, one-handed, and stood there a while.
You're doing it right, my lord. The worst part of it. You're doing it right.
When I woke, a letter lay by my hand, on violet paper that smelled of expensive perfume. Lady Sabine Corrow was collecting her favour.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter one hundred and thirty, coming soon.
